what_this_is: How to teach anyone to dance, as far as the nightly study has come. Use 'default' as the way to teach, 'moments' at the points that decide whether a learner stays, 'when_it_is_hard' and 'when_a_feeling_shows' to answer the person, and 'remember' over time. It is evidence, not a verdict: watched and read by a machine, not checked by a person, not tested on learners. The whole study with its proof is in bdf_teaching_system.json.

default.do: Show the step from behind or mirrored, so it can be copied directly.
Show the whole thing once at speed before breaking it down.
Teach one small piece at a time and practise it before adding the next.
Feet first; add arms, styling and turns only when the feet are steady.
Start slow and speed up in steps to full tempo.
Count out loud or speak the rhythm.
Bring in the music early, not only at the end.
Repeat more than feels necessary, with follow-along rounds.
End with a recap and one small practice to take away.
Give an image to aim at instead of a muscle to control.
Teach the feeling and the bounce before precision.
Invite the learner to vary it and make it their own.
Open or close with a moment to arrive: breath, music, thanks.
Get the learner dancing something real in the first minutes.
Tell learners they can do it, and name each small win.
Treat mistakes as normal, and show your own.
Bring humour and visible joy.
Offer choices: the tempo, the variation, when to pause.
Connect the learner with others: a partner, a challenge, something to share.
Give a reason to come back: the next step, a series, a routine.
Name the common mistake and show the fix.
Offer an easier version the moment a step is hard.
Offer a harder version to those who are ready.
Give options for different bodies, small rooms and no partner.
Teach learners how to check themselves.
Say what the learner may be feeling, and answer it.
Share your own beginnings and struggles.
Say, and show, that dance belongs to everybody.
Treat the learner as a dancer from the first minute.
Ask the learner to notice how it felt.
Give permission to pause and to come back tomorrow.

moments.title: How they open
teachers_do: Greets the viewers and introduces shuffle dance basics specifically tailored for older adults and those finding it difficult to train.
The teacher introduces the lesson, listing the turns to be covered and inviting the learner to find a space to move.
The teacher introduces the lesson as a social dance session, emphasizing that it is not about technique but about learning how to dance simply and easily.

moments.title: Before a hard part
teachers_do: The teacher offers a simplified starting point on the spot if learners struggle at first.
The teacher explains the correct knee alignment for a plié, emphasizing the importance of not overextending.
The teacher asks the learner to imagine being in a social situation where everyone is dancing, and they are watching, wishing they could join in.

moments.title: After a mistake
teachers_do: The teacher shares her own past confusion about the term 'close your ribcage' to make the concept relatable and less intimidating.
The teacher tells the learner to lift their legs to see the steps more clearly, framing the adjustment as a way to make the learning process easier.
The teacher says it can get confusing if you don't do it lots of times, and then repeats the sequence.

moments.title: After a success
teachers_do: The teacher encourages the learner and expresses hope that the explanation was clear.
The teacher tells the learner they are doing great and that if they can do this, they can definitely dance.
The teacher confirms the steps are taught and reminds the learner to add the quarter turn at the end.

moments.title: Checking in
teachers_do: The teacher encourages the learner to return to the basics if they feel lost or overwhelmed during the turn breakdown.
Maybe pause this video, put yourself some music on and practice this first movement.
The teacher asks the learner if they are managing to follow the steps and encourages them to keep going.

moments.title: How they close
teachers_do: The teacher transitions the learner into practicing the full sequence along with the music.
The teacher invites the learner to check out their website for more in-depth dancing programs if they want to learn more technique.
The teacher encourages the learner to try the dance and watch the next demo to see what song to use.

in_their_words: Dancing and learning shuffle moves are accessible to older adults and those who find training difficult.
Anyone can look cool and confident at a party, even if they do not know how to dance initially.
Dancing is for social situations, like weddings and parties, where you can have fun with others.
Line dancing is versatile and can be performed to almost any country song.
Repetition is the mother of learning for building muscle memory in the body.
Consistent practice and patience are the keys to overcoming initial difficulties in learning to dance.
The teacher's role is to help people learn to dance simply and socially, not to teach complex technique.
A teacher acts as a role model who must act respectfully and teach others who want to learn.
